title: BNP Veteran Mirza Fakhrul Islam Alamgir Elected as Bangladesh's 23rd President
excerpt: The 78-year-old former BNP secretary general won a decisive parliamentary vote, marking the first contested presidential election in Bangladesh in 35 years.
body:
• BNP veteran Mirza Fakhrul Islam Alamgir elected as Bangladesh's 23rd president with 255 votes against rival Oli Ahmad's 88
  • The 78-year-old former BNP secretary general will be sworn in on Friday, filling the vacancy left by Mohammed Shahabuddin's resignation in July
  • The contested presidential election was the first in Bangladesh in 35 years, with voting held among 349 eligible MPs
  • The presidency is largely ceremonial but carries constitutional weight as head of state and commander-in-chief of the armed forces

Bangladesh's parliament elected veteran politician Mirza Fakhrul Islam Alamgir as the country's 23rd president on Thursday, capping a political transition that has reshaped the South Asian nation's leadership since the fall of Sheikh Hasina's Awami League government in 2024.

A Decisive Victory in a Rare Contest

Alamgir, 78, secured 255 votes in the parliamentary ballot, comfortably defeating Oli Ahmad, 84, the retired army colonel and Liberal Democratic Party chairman backed by an 11-party opposition alliance led by Jamaat-e-Islami. Ahmad received 88 votes. Of the 349 eligible members of parliament, 343 cast valid ballots during the three-hour voting window in the Jatiya Sangsad chamber.

The contest marked Bangladesh's first contested presidential election in 35 years. In a parliamentary system where the ruling party typically commands enough seats to make the outcome a formality, the BNP's two-thirds majority in parliament following the February 2026 general election ensured Alamgir's victory was never seriously in doubt.

"I want Bangladesh to become a more prosperous and welfare-oriented country, with greater attention given to marginalised communities, workers and low-income households."

— Mirza Fakhrul Islam Alamgir, ahead of the vote

From Left-Wing Activist to Presidential Palace

Alamgir's path to Bangladesh's highest office spans more than five decades of political life. Born in Thakurgaon on January 26, 1948, he studied economics at the University of Dhaka, where he joined the left-leaning East Pakistan Students Union during the 1969 mass upsurge against Pakistani military rule.

He emerged as a prominent organizer of freedom fighters during the 1971 Liberation War before pivoting to academia, teaching economics at government colleges including Dhaka College. His transition from the civil service to frontline politics came through the BNP, where he rose to become secretary general — a position he held until resigning to stand for the presidency on August 13.

He has previously held government portfolios covering local government, agriculture, aviation, and tourism. Most recently, he served as the minister for local government, rural development, and cooperatives in the government of Prime Minister Tarique Rahman.

Filling a Constitutional Vacancy

The election was triggered by the resignation of former president Mohammed Shahabuddin on July 24, who stepped down two years before the end of his term citing serious health concerns. Bangladesh's constitution requires a replacement to be elected within 90 days of a vacancy.

Although the presidency is largely ceremonial under Bangladesh's parliamentary system, the position carries constitutional significance. The president serves as head of state and commander-in-chief of the armed forces, with powers to appoint the chief justice and dissolve parliament under certain conditions.

What It Means for Bangladesh's Direction

Alamgir's election consolidates BNP's grip on all branches of government following the political upheaval that began with mass student protests against Hasina's government in 2024. The BNP secured a commanding parliamentary majority in the February 2026 election, installing Tarique Rahman as prime minister.

The newly elected president is scheduled to take the oath of office on Friday evening at Bangabhaban, the presidential palace in Dhaka. His immediate priorities, as outlined before the vote, center on economic welfare and social inclusion — themes that echo the BNP's broader governance agenda as it navigates Bangladesh's post-transition political landscape.
